lessons.title: Inventory costs and the EOQ model

topics.title: What inventory is and what it costs
topics.what: Inventory is the stock of materials a firm holds to meet future demand: raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods and MRO supplies.
topics.why: Firms hold it to meet anticipated demand, decouple production stages, protect against stock-outs, use quantity discounts and hedge against price rises.
topics.how: Three costs matter: ordering cost S per order (independent of order size), holding cost H per unit per year, and shortage cost. Big orders cut ordering cost but raise holding cost; small orders do the opposite.
topics.business_use: Every distributor or retailer decides how much to reorder; getting the balance wrong either ties up cash in stock or causes frequent ordering and stock-outs.
advantages: Protects service levels and smooths production
limitations: Inventory ties up capital and carries holding costs such as storage, insurance and obsolescence
remember: Ordering cost is per order and does not depend on order size
Holding cost is per unit per year
Inventory management balances ordering cost against holding cost

definitions.text: The stock of materials a firm holds to meet future demand.
Cost of placing and receiving one order; it does not depend on order size.
Cost of keeping one unit in stock for one year.
Lost sales and goodwill when demand cannot be met.

topics.title: The EOQ model
topics.what: EOQ is the order quantity that minimises total annual ordering plus holding cost.
topics.why: It gives a simple, calculable answer to 'how much should we order each time?'
topics.how: Total cost TC = (D/Q)S + (Q/2)H is lowest where ordering cost equals holding cost, which gives EOQ = sqrt(2DS/H).
topics.business_use: Used to set standard order sizes for items with steady demand.
advantages: Total cost curve is flat near the EOQ, so small rounding barely changes cost
limitations: Assumes known, constant demand and lead time, instant delivery, no quantity discounts and no shortages
remember: At the EOQ, annual ordering cost = annual holding cost

definitions.text: The order quantity that minimises total annual ordering and holding cost.

supplementary: Observation that the total-cost curve is flat near its minimum (read from the curve)

topics.title: Worked example: EOQ
topics.what: A distributor with D = 12,000 units, S = Rs 500, H = Rs 30 and 300 working days.
topics.why: Shows each step of applying the EOQ formulas.
topics.how: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 12,000 x 500 / 30) = 632.46 units; N = 18.97 orders; 15.8 days between orders; TC = Rs 18,973.67.
topics.business_use: Turns the formula into an ordering policy: about 632 units roughly every 16 working days.
advantages: Checks itself: ordering cost equals holding cost at the answer
limitations: Answers are rounded in practice (632 units, 19 orders)
remember: About 19 orders a year, about 16 working days apart
TC = Rs 18,973.67, half ordering and half holding

lessons.title: When to reorder and what to control

topics.title: Reorder point and safety stock
topics.what: The reorder point is the inventory level at which a new order is placed: ROP = d x L + SS.
topics.why: EOQ says how much to order; the ROP says when, so that stock arrives before it runs out.
topics.how: Multiply daily demand by lead time in days and add safety stock kept against uncertainty in demand or lead time.
topics.business_use: Stores and warehouses set a trigger level in their system: when stock falls to it, a purchase order goes out.

definitions.text: The inventory level at which a new order is placed.
Extra stock kept to protect against uncertainty in demand or lead time.

topics.title: ABC analysis
topics.what: A classification of items by annual consumption value (annual demand x unit cost), following the Pareto principle.
topics.why: Management attention is limited, so it should go to the few items that carry most of the value.
topics.how: Class A: 10-20% of items, 70-80% of value, tight control. Class B: about 30% of items, 15-25% of value. Class C: 50-60% of items, 5-10% of value, simple control.
topics.business_use: Decides review frequency and control effort per item.
advantages: Focuses control effort where the money is
limitations: Looks only at value: a cheap item can still be critical, so ABC is combined with VED analysis
remember: A items: few items, most of the value
Combine ABC with VED (Vital, Essential, Desirable)

definitions.text: Classification of inventory items by annual consumption value (annual demand x unit cost).
Classification of items as Vital, Essential or Desirable, used alongside ABC.

practice.question: Annual demand is 8,000 units, ordering cost is Rs 400 per order and holding cost is Rs 25 per unit per year. Find the EOQ.
For the question above, how many orders are placed per year?
Daily demand is 50 units, lead time is 4 days and safety stock is 80 units. What is the reorder point?
Why is the total annual cost at the EOQ split equally between ordering and holding cost?
practice.answer: Because total cost is minimum where the falling ordering-cost curve and the rising holding-cost curve are equal; the notes state this on page 4 and the example on page 5 confirms it (Rs 9,486.83 each).

practice.question: A spare part costs very little but its absence stops the production line. How would ABC and VED analysis classify it, and what should the firm do?
practice.answer: ABC would put it in class C (low value), but VED would mark it Vital; the notes say ABC should be combined with VED, so the firm should keep it well stocked despite its low value.
